Introduction

The assessment of impairment associated with chronic pain creates vexing problems for any impair-ment rating system. Experts have disagreed about the usefulness and questioned the validity of the rating systems for pain-related impairment (PRI) described in previous editions of the Guides, and these dif-ficulties have continued throughout the development of the current chapter.

Several factors contribute to the controversies that have surrounded PRI:

• There are fundamental conceptual problems when pain is construed as a cause of impairment, pri-marily because there is no objective way to quan-tify pain or its variable effects on the individual.

• Empirical data are sparse about the role of pain in impairment. As a result, both proponents and opponents of PRI must rely on rhetoric rather than scientific data when they support their positions.

• Whereas much of the AMA Guides’ system reflects consensus among experts in various areas of medi-cine, consensus about the appropriate role of PRI

has been lacking. At one extreme, some experts in pain medicine have argued that PRI should be given a prominent role in the Guides, and that the PRI rating system should permit high percentages of whole person impairment (WPI) to be awarded for chronic pain. In contrast, others have argued that PRI should be dispensed with altogether.

• The arguments for and against the inclusion of PRI in the Guides have not been articulated in pub-lished articles and thus have not been subjected to the public scrutiny that would be expected for such an important topic. A consequence is that the pres-ent authors have had to rely primarily on informal data sources as we discuss the arguments for and against PRI.

3.1 Definition and Classification of Pain

3.1a Definition of Pain

The International Association Study of Pain defines pain as “an unpleasant sensory and emotional expe-rience associated with actual or potential tissue dam-age or described in terms of such damage.”1 Pain is a prominent symptom in many acute injuries and illnesses, and often subsides as the medical condi-tion resolves. Since such acute pain is usually short lived, it is not a problem that is considered in an impairment rating system. However, chronic pain is a problem that potentially could be the cause for an impairment rating. The definition of chronic pain is imprecise but, in a general way, it refers to pain that persists over time. For the purposes of the Guides, chronic pain is defined as pain that persists beyond the expected healing time of the medical disorder thought to have initiated the pain. For many sections in the Guides, chronic pain will be pain that per-sists beyond 3 months, as most common conditions affecting the musculoskeletal and other organ sys-tems will substantially heal in this time frame. The nervous system is a notable exception. Although any time point is arbitrary, 3 months should encompass the expected healing time in most situations where there is tissue injury but will allow for situations in which there is no expected healing time.2

3.1b Chronic Pain Syndrome

In both the Fourth and Fifth Editions of the Guides, a definition of chronic pain syndrome (CPS) was included that captured the major biopsychosocial characteristics of chronic pain. Indeed, the biopsy-chosocial approach to chronic pain and disability is

currently viewed as the most heuristic perspective to the understanding, assessment, and treatment of chronic pain disorders, and has replaced the outdated biomedical reductionist perspective.3–7 This biopsy-chosocial approach views chronic pain as a complex and dynamic interaction among biological, psycho-logical, and social factors that perpetuates, and may even worsen, the clinical presentation. Each person will experience a chronic pain condition uniquely, thus accounting for the great individual differences in how pain is expressed. The complexity of a chronic pain disorder is especially evident when it persists over time, as a range of psychosocial and economic factors can interact with pathophysiology to modu-late a patient’s report of discomfort and disability associated with chronic pain. Moreover, even as healing occurs, all patients experience some degree of physical deconditioning associated with stiffness and muscle atrophy in the injured area. Risk factors for profound deconditioning with the injured area becoming a “weak link” include extended periods of inactivity, inhibition of function due to pain, and fear avoidance. In striking contrast, the traditional and outdated biomedical approach assumes that all pain symptoms have specific physical causes, and attempts to eradicate the cause directly by identifying and rectifying the presumed pathophysiology. However, chronic pain can rarely be understood by the linear, nociceptive mechanism. As will be discussed later in this chapter, there is often an absence of a document-able relationship between pain and pathophysiology.

With the above biopsychosocial perspective in mind, CPS can be described as pain that continues beyond the normal healing time for the patient’s diagnosis and includes significant psychosocial dysfunction. It should be noted that this definition does not include any specific time frame to use in making the diagnosis of CPS. This omission is intentional and reflects clinical reality, in that some conditions would be expected to resolve in several days and others in several months or even years. The diagnosis of CPS should then be tem-porally connected to the point at which a given con-dition or conditions were expected to have resolved, rather than to any arbitrary time period for an injury or event. Regardless of when it occurs, CPS is a condition that ultimately adversely affects the patient’s well-being, level of function, and quality of life. The major characteristics associated with CPS include the follow-ing, with 3 or more required for a diagnosis:

• Use of prescription drugs beyond the recom-mended duration and/or abuse of or dependence on prescription drugs or other substances.

• Excessive dependence on health care providers, spouse, or family.

3.1d Neuropathic Pain

Traditionally, neuropathic pain has been defined as pain caused by abnormal function of the nervous system due to injury or disease. A key feature of neuropathic pain is that, although an affected indi-vidual perceives pain as emanating from some bodily structure (eg, the distal lower extremity in sciatica, the radial aspect of the hand in carpal tunnel syndrome), the pathophysiologic basis for the pain is an abnor-mality in the functioning of the nervous system, rather than an abnormality in the “end-organ” where the pain is perceived. Thus, the simple relation between end-organ damage and pain perception found in noci-ceptive pain is absent in neuropathic pain.

Neurobiologic research during the past 20 years has conclusively demonstrated that injury and accom-panying nociception can induce functional changes in the nervous system that lead to something akin to neuropathic pain. Activation of peripheral nocicep-tive nerve fibers almost immediately modifies the nerve’s response to further stimuli. Nociceptive stim-ulation results in the release of neurotransmitters and peptides that increase the excitability or “sensitize” sensory neurons.9 This peripheral sensitization is associated with an increased sensitivity to mechani-cal and thermal stimuli, and results in reports of pain to normally nonpainful stimuli (allodynia) and an increase in the magnitude of pain caused by noxious stimuli (hyperalgesia). Increased input from periph-eral nociceptive neurons, in turn, leads to alterations in the spinal cord dorsal horn, both disinhibition and increased responsiveness of central neurons.10 This central sensitization can lead to a number of symptoms and signs, including spontaneous pain, spreading pain, and hypersensitivity to touch and extremes of temperature. Indeed, such increased responsiveness to stimuli has been demonstrated in patients with chronic pain following whiplash injury and in those with fibromyalgia.11 The processes of peripheral and central sensitization are a normal consequence of tissue injury, and they offer signifi-cant protection to the organism; after tissue injury, sensitization serves as a reminder that the region is injured and should be closely guarded until the tissue has healed. However, the same neuronal mechanisms can lead to persistent pain even after all evidence of the initial inciting disease or injury have resolved. This persistent sensitization can subserve pain per-ceptions that share key features with neuropathic pain as defined above, including:

• Spontaneous Pain—pain that occurs without a specific sensory stimulus (eg, the sudden lanci-nating pain described by those with postherpetic neuralgia).

• Paresthesias/dysesthesias—abnormal pain dis-tant from the site of actual tissue injury that may be spontaneous or evoked (eg, the radiating pain associated with lumbar nerve root compression).

• Hyperalgesia—an exaggerated painful response to a normally noxious stimulus (eg, light pinprick leads to extreme and prolonged pain).

• Allodynia—a painful response to a normally nonnoxious stimulus (eg, light touch causes pain).

Pain specialists and neurobiologists are divided on the question of whether pain secondary to nervous system sensitization, such as that believed to occur in patients with fibromyalgia, should be construed as a form of neuropathic pain.12 For purposes of rating PRI, however, pain associated with nervous system sensitization is similar to neuropathic pain in that an individual’s perceptions of pain are dis-sociated from end-organ injury or dysfunction. If anything, pain associated with nervous system sen-sitization is even more elusive than traditional neu-ropathic pain. The reason for this is that, although the link between end-organ dysfunction and pain is severed in neuropathic pain, there is typically objectively measurable damage to the nervous sys-tem. In contrast, individuals suffering from pain associated with nervous system sensitization fre-quently do not have objective evidence of damage or dysfunction, either in the end-organ where the pain is perceived or in the nervous system.

3.1e Persistent Pain as a Disease Entity

Persistent pain is a major health problem, with between 18% and 50% of the population report-ing continuous pain for at least 3 of the last 6 months.13–15 Chronic pain has been linked with significant disability.16 Although pain has been traditionally regarded as a symptom that serves as a warning signal of an underlying disease process, there is accumulating evidence that persistent pain should be considered a disease entity in its own right.2 Indeed, permanent changes in the respon-siveness of both the peripheral and central nervous systems can persist even after all tissue healing has ensued; thus, persistent pain can become a self-perpetuating condition. The individual is often left with ongoing pain without identifiable signs of the original inciting disease process that initiated the pain. This results in a multitude of consequences that can lead to significant impair-ment for the individual affected, including physi-cal impairment, mood dysfunction, and social disruption. This is in keeping with the earlier bio-psychosocial perspective of CPS.

3.2 Controversies Surrounding Pain-Related Impairment

3.2a Practical Problems With Rating Pain-Related Impairment

Subjectivity of Pain

Impairment is defined in Chapter 1 of the Guides as “a significant deviation, loss, or loss of use, of any body structure or body function in an individual with a health condition, disorder, or disease.” An impairment rating is defined as a “consensus-derived percentage estimate of loss, which reflects severity of impairment for a given health condition, and the degree of associated limitations in terms of ADLs” as traditionally defined by the domains of personal mobility and self-care.

As these definitions indicate, impairments are viewed as biomedical abnormalities that can be analyzed at the level of organs or body parts. Also, the implicit assumption throughout the Guides is that impairments should be assessed on the basis of objective medical data, rather than on the basis of the self-reporting of patients. Thus, for example, a physician could assess renal impairment on the basis of creatinine clearance or cardiac impairment on the basis of ejection fraction.

A key feature of pain is its subjectivity. Physicians and other observers can make inferences about a patient’s pain but cannot directly experience it. To examine the significance of this feature of pain, it is useful to conceptually divide factors that might be considered in impairment ratings into 2 groups: (1) objective factors such as atrophy of a limb or reduced ejection fraction and (2) subjective factors such as pain. Whereas objective medical factors are assessed via methods (eg, laboratory assays or imaging studies) that are unrelated to the subjec-tive experiences and communications of a patient, the assessment of subjective factors requires an examiner to interpret the communications of the patient, and to use these communications to infer the patient’s subjective experiences.

In terms of the dichotomy between objective and subjective factors, the Guides strive to base impair-ment ratings on objective factors insofar as possible. This principle is violated by any system that rates impairment associated with pain. Some experts argue that such a violation represents a fundamental deviation from the central purpose of the Guides and question why the basic logic of the Guides should be compromised in order to include pain in impairment ratings.

Pain is the subjective factor that is considered in this chapter for the practical reason that it is the one most commonly encountered when impairment ratings according to the Guides are performed. However, it is not the only subjective factor that can contribute to the burden of illness imposed by a medical condi-tion. For example, in addition to pain, the burden of illness associated with medical disorders can be increased by other subjective factors such as fatigue or emotional distress. Moreover, psychiatric disor-ders are characterized by subjective processes such as anxiety or hallucinations that are not amenable to assessment via objective methods such as laboratory or imaging studies. Thus, the challenge of assessing subjective factors is crucial to the determination of impairment associated with mental illness.

Level of Analysis: Body Parts vs Whole Person

Another conceptual problem with any PRI is that pain and its effects need to be analyzed at the level of the whole person, rather than at the level of a spe-cific organ or body part. People with chronic pain typically attribute their pain and activity limitations to dysfunction of an organ or body part. But these subjective reports are difficult to assess precisely because examination of the involved organ or body part often does not identify abnormalities that make the pain reports inevitable.17 It often appears to an observer that the affected organ or body part is capable of functioning, but that the patient does not use it normally because of pain. In keeping with the biopsychosocial perspective, the observer must con-sider the person as a whole in order to make sense of the situation. Thus, the assessment of incapacitation secondary to pain violates the tenet that impair-ment evaluations should assess the functioning of organs or body parts, rather than the functioning of an individual as a whole. However, this tenet, which is based on the outdated biomedical reductionist approach, needs to be seriously questioned in light of the more recent heuristic biopsychosocial approach to chronic pain.

Pain as Isolated Problem vs Component of Medical Conditions

Another conceptual challenge related to PRI is that pain is not something completely distinct from organ or body part dysfunction. Rather, it is usually most appro-priate to construe pain as a “component” of a medi-cal disorder. From this perspective, it is arbitrary to examine the significance of pain in isolation from the medical condition underlying the pain, just as it would be arbitrary to evaluate shortness of breath in isolation from congestive heart failure. It would be more concep-tually appropriate to evaluate a medical disorder as an

entity with characteristic signs, symptoms, pathophysi-ology, and potential organ or body part dysfunction. An impairment rating based on such an evaluation would take into account all the manifestations of the disor-der, including pain. In fact, this edition of the Guides does, for the most part, construe pain as one of many manifestations of injuries or diseases, and impairment ratings attempt to take into account the pain that typi-cally occurs in various disorders. Unfortunately, this intuitively plausible approach to incorporating pain into impairment ratings sometimes runs into either of 2 complicating situations. First, it may well be the case that pain severity does not correlate well with objective indicators of organ or body part dysfunction. In fact, empirical scientific research has consistently demon-strated that there is often a low concordance or correla-tion among self-report of pain, behavioral functioning such as ADLs, and physiologic indexes.3,18 In such a situation, impairment ratings based strictly on objective factors are likely to fail to capture the burden of illness of the disorder.

A second and more difficult situation is that some conditions are associated with severe pain but are not amenable to conventional impairment ratings because they are not associated with unequivocal objective factors. In these conditions, it is not possi-ble to make impairment ratings on the basis of objec-tive factors. Common examples include headache disorders and fibromyalgia.

Resolution of Conceptual Conundrums

Some people might conclude that the problems listed in this section are conceptual conundrums that preclude the incorporation of PRI into the Guides’ system. However, we believe that the conceptual foundation of the AMA Guides (as articulated in Chapters 1 and 2) is compatible with the inclusion of PRI as long as certain clarifications are made. A key to the resolution of the conceptual issues described earlier comes from close inspection of the definition of an impairment rating as a “consensus-derived percentage estimate of loss of activity reflecting severity for a given health condition, and the degree of associated limitations in terms of ADLs” as tradi-tionally defined by the domains of personal mobility and self-care. This definition implies that severity of impairment depends on 2 criteria: (1) the severity of dysfunction in the relevant organ or body part and (2) the extent to which the condition being evalu-ated affects the ability of the individual to perform ADLs. Chronic pain can reasonably be interpreted as a factor that causes deficits in an individual’s abil-ity to perform ADLs, even in settings where objec-tive indicators of organ or body part dysfunction are modest or even nonexistent. Thus, we believe that

the inclusion of PRI in the Guides is compatible with the overall conceptualization of the AMA system presented in Chapters 1 and 2.

3.2b Fundamental Concepts in Determining Pain-Related Impairment

Specious Issues

Even if one accepts the premise that PRI can be construed as a type of impairment because pain can diminish an individual’s ability to perform ADLs, several arguments against the inclusion of a system for rating PRI can be raised. As discussed below, we consider some of these arguments to be specious, but others to be crucial. Arguments that have been raised by proponents and opponents of including PRI in the Guides are described in Appendix 3-3 at the end of this chapter.

• The argument that PRI should not be included in the Guides because of the subjectivity of pain is a theoretical one, related to the fundamental purpose of the Guides. If this purpose is solely to evaluate an abstract construct labeled “impairment,” the argument is valid. However, we believe that the ultimate purpose of impairment rating is to deter-mine the burden of illness borne by individuals with various medical problems, so that they can be compensated fairly. The burden of illness associ-ated with a medical condition is best approximated by the impact of the condition on an individual’s ability to perform ADLs. From this perspective, all factors that influence ADLs—including subjec-tive ones—should, in principle, be included in the AMA system.

• The argument that PRI should not be included in the AMA system because of a lack of empirical evidence sounds plausible but is actually specious when one considers the Guides as a whole. The key issue is that most of the conventional ratings in the Guides are not validated by empirical research. Although the goal of buttressing impairment rat-ings on the basis of empirical research is laudable, this goal should not be applied selectively to the assessment of PRI.

• Most pain specialists would challenge the argu-ment that PRI is unnecessary because conventional ratings in the Guides already include pain. As discussed below, we believe that the conventional rating system does provide appropriate ratings for many patients with chronic pain. However, the problem of PRI cannot be dismissed completely, because some painful conditions cannot be rated on the basis of the conventional system.

• The argument that a PRI rating system might cause problems for the insurance industry may well be valid, but we believe that the need for a system that fairly compensates individuals with long-term func-tional deficits outweighs the desire of the insurance industry to simplify their benefit packages.

• We agree with the argument that the PRI system described in the Guides’ Fifth Edition was overly complex and believe that this practical concern should inform the development of the PRI assess-ment system for the Sixth Edition. However, we do not believe that this practical concern bears on the fundamental question of whether the Guides should include a PRI rating.

Crucial Issues

In our opinion, the most powerful arguments against the inclusion of PRI in the Guides are that (1) PRI assessments are likely to be unreliable and (2) they might lead to systematic errors in assess-ment, such that persuasive patients can “game the system” and get inappropriately high impairment awards. Both of these arguments derive from the premise that it is very difficult for examiners to determine the extent to which patients are affected by their pain. These difficulties were succinctly captured by Scarry19 when she said: “To have great pain is to have certainty; to hear that another person has pain is to have doubt.” The problem of reliabil-ity and validity of PRI assessment is much more than an academic problem in measurement theory. The Guides serves the societal role of providing an equitable method of compensating individuals whose ability to function has been compromised by a medical condition. For the Guides to carry out this role, it must be perceived as fair. To be per-ceived as fair, the Guides must employ assessment procedures that are reliable and valid, rather than capricious ones that can be manipulated by persua-sive patients. Thus, regardless of how severely pain affects individuals with various medical conditions, a PRI assessment system must have reasonable reli-ability and validity to accomplish the societal goal of fairly compensating them.

In fact, the key issue separating proponents and opponents of impairment due to pain is the weight they place on ease of measurement of PRI vs relevance of PRI. Advocates for PRI emphasize that pain has great relevance to the ability to function of individuals who have various medical conditions, but these advocates tend to downplay the problems of measuring PRI. Opponents tend to emphasize problems in measurement but ignore the issue of relevance. In principle, empirical research could be

performed to determine the strength of the indepen-dent contribution that pain makes to the burden of illness borne by individuals with various medical conditions, and whether examiners can reliably and validly assess PRI. Considerable research has been done on the first issue, at least for some common painful conditions such as disorders of the lumbar spine. Unfortunately, though, essentially no research has been done on the issue of determining the reli-ability and validity of PRI assessments. Construct validation research is greatly needed in this area. At this time, as a practical matter, decisions regarding PRI for purposes of the Guides’ Sixth Edition must be based on judgment rather than empirical data.

How Much Weight Should Be Given to Pain in Impairment Ratings?

Whether or not to include PRI in the Guides can be framed as a qualitative yes or no question. However, it is more fruitful to frame the issue in quantitative terms by asking the following question: How much weight should be given to pain in impairment rat-ings? Opponents of PRI, in effect, argue that pain (and other subjective factors) should be given zero weight, so that impairment ratings reflect only objec-tive factors. Many proponents of including PRI in the Guides argue not only that pain should be considered in impairment ratings but also that a PRI system should permit patients with severe pain to receive impairment awards with high WPI percentages. An impairment rating system could make a “cautious foray into the difficult waters” of PRI assessment by permitting awards to be made for PRI, but cap-ping these awards at a modest level. This describes the strategy used in the Guides’ Fifth Edition, in which PRI was capped at 3% WPI. In the absence of persuasive empirical research on the extent to which pain affects the ability of people with medical condi-tions to function or the measurement problems that arise when PRI is assessed, any decision about caps for PRI will be perceived as arbitrary.

3.3 The Rating System

3.3a The Problem of Credibility and Consistency in Rating Pain-Related Impairment

Whenever examiners conduct impairment evalu-ations, they must consider the consistency and interpretability of the clinical data for a patient. For example, a primary step in radiographic interpreta-tion is an evaluation of the quality of the image.

Incorrect exposure, motion artifact, and other techni-cal deficiencies (including poor interrater reliability between radiologists reading the radiographs) may weaken the conclusions that can be drawn from it. More generally, examiners using the techniques described in Chapters 4 to 17 must consider whether diagnostic studies have been performed appropri-ately, and whether a patient presents with a coherent set of symptoms and signs that clearly point to the diagnosis of a well-accepted medical condition.

Most experts believe that the problem of interpreting clinical data is greater for patients undergoing PRI assessment than for ones being rated according to principles in Chapters 4 to 17. The principal gauge of pain is its associated behaviors, which include verbal reports and nonverbal pain behaviors such as limping. The challenge for an examiner is to decide whether these pain behaviors accurately reflect a patient’s experiences. Inappropriate pain behavior, embellishment, and symptom magnification are not uncommon, particularly in medicolegal circum-stances and entitlement programs. In evaluating the reliability and credibility of pain behaviors among patients undergoing PRI assessments, examiners should consider the following:

• Congruence with established conditions.

• Consistency over time and situation.

• Consistency with anatomy and physiology.

• Agreement between observers.

• Inappropriate illness behavior.

Congruence With Established Conditions

In phantom pain, the patient describes pain in an absent extremity. While this might be expected to evoke incredulity, it does not, because this condition has been well described for decades, long before its pathophysiology was understood. Similarly, the person with complex regional pain syndrome (previously called reflex sympathetic dystrophy, Sudek’s disuse atrophy, or causalgia) may describe exquisite pain on light touch of a healthy appearing extremity following a trivial injury. A constellation of associated signs and symptoms, such as cold sensitivity, autonomic changes, trophic changes, dystonic phenomena, and others help to confirm that the pain complaint is consistent with a known clinical syndrome. Intolerance of light touch over a region of the lower back in patients with mechanical low back pain is not consistent with a defined disease process and thus fails to meet this criterion. Most known condi-tions have such expected concomitants. Typically,

a patient would not watch television or read while waiting for a migraine to abate, and there would be an expected response to ergots, triptans, or other antimigraine preparations. A patient with neuropathic pain would likely, but not always, show some response to certain antiepileptic drugs (eg, gabapentin, carbamazepine) or antidepressants (eg, tricyclics). A person with persistent pain of pancreatitis would be unlikely to gain weight.

Consistency Over Time and Situation

There is a risk of placing unwarranted confidence in the validity of assessments that are numeri-cal and therefore often considered “objective” and “scientific.” Such confidence is challenged by such observations as a person who can tolerate only 10° forward flexion while standing, yet can sit with legs outstretched and touch his or her toes. Similarly, a person may demonstrate collapsing with pain on manual testing of plantar flexion, yet be able to tiptoe. Others may limp on one leg walking for-ward, the other walking backward, and not at all on a treadmill. Grip strength may be measured repeatedly and coefficients of variation calculated, although these methods have been criticized.20 Rapid exchange grip strength testing may provide similar information.21 Isokinetic strength testing may dis-criminate between maximal and submaximal effort.17 Complaints and dysfunction should be relatively independent of the observers present and should generally persist despite distraction.

Consistency With Anatomy and Physiology

One would expect a patient who claims to be unable to use an arm at all to show some signs of atrophy or decreased muscle tone. A patient with inability to bear weight on one leg or who has a limp should show evidence of differential shoe wear patterns. Although evaluating whether there is clear physical evidence of pain-related dysfunction is ideal, there are also numerous “tests” that can be performed to assess whether pain behaviors are more likely to be accounted for by patient expectations than by organic pathology, with Waddell’s signs perhaps the best known of these indicators.22,23 One example is that of axial rotation, in which the standing patient’s hips are rotated in each direction by the examiner. This essentially affects only the hips and ankles, leaving the pelvis and all above it to move as a unit. Exacerbation of back pain by this maneuver is con-sidered abnormal. It is important, however, when using this method to rate the patient not on one abnormal test only, and to place the response in the context of the totality of the patient’s history, physi-cal examination findings, and cultural background.

Interobserver Agreement

Collateral information from relatives and other evalu-ating professionals is of critical value in determining the consistency of patient behaviors. This information may confirm that a patient’s pain behaviors reflect a relationship to perceived pain, and that they vary lit-tle with changes in observers. Alternatively, the infor-mation may expose major inconsistencies that raise questions about the factors underlying the patient’s pain behaviors.

Inappropriate Illness Behavior

It may be difficult to judge whether behavior is compatible with perceived pain. For example, since one cannot know how much leg pain a patient expe-riences on walking, it is hard to know whether an antalgic gait is exaggerated. Inappropriate illness behavior may be suspected, however, if the patient demonstrates dysfunction in unrelated domains. For example, except in extreme situations, a patient with back pain should not require that the spouse complete the patient’s questionnaire—or his or her sentences. Chronic pain does not often preclude making one’s own phone calls to the doctor, paying bills, and so forth. When a person has delegated these functions to others, abnormal illness behavior is likely.

The PRI assessment system described in this chapter assigns a presumptive impairment rating based on self-report data by a patient. Examiners are asked to modify this rating on the basis of their clinical judgment regarding the consistency and reliability of these self-report data. Examiners are advised to consider the issues outlined above when they make these judgments. A word of caution is in order here. Although no one would conclude that, because an X ray was of poor quality, there was unlikely to be pathology of concern, this non sequitur frequently occurs in the case of aberrant pain behaviors. Such behaviors should properly cause the physician to be uncertain but not automatically dismissive. Behavior is affected by many factors. As discussed earlier, the heuristic biopsychosocial approach to pain would predict differences in pain behavior across individu-als because of unique interactions among physical, psychological, and social factors that become even more complex when pain is chronic. The appear-ance of symptom exaggeration can be created by fear or by having learned that certain actions or positions provoke pain. “Nonphysiologic” signs may occur in dementia. Excessive or exaggerated pain behaviors can be a response to feeling discounted or mistrusted, so that one must emphasize symptoms to persuade the physician of their reality. Anyone might dramatize a problem in an effort to have it taken

seriously. Thus, symptom magnification can be an iatrogenic phenomenon that occurs when patients feel mistrusted or poorly cared for.

3.3b Rating Impairment When Pain Accompanies Objective Findings of Injury or Illness That Permit Rating Using Another Chapter in the Guides

The PRI system that was developed for the Sixth Edition of the Guides makes a basic distinction between assessing pain in conditions that can be rated according to principles outlined in Chapters 4 through 17, vs ones that cannot be rated. The PRI system outlined in this chapter is used only if a patient presents with a painful condition and cannot be rated according to principles outlined in Chapters 4 to 17. It should also be noted that patients’ subjective experiences regarding their conditions are considered in the ratings described in Chapters 4 to 17. Specifically, patients are asked to fill out functional assessment instruments in which they indicate the impact of their condition on their ability to function. Although responses to such instruments reflect a variety of factors, it is assumed that pain will influence them. Thus, we believe that the impairment ratings described in the remaining chapters of this book can capture the burden imposed by pain that is construed as a component of a ratable disorder. As discussed in Chapter 1, patients’ responses on functional assessment instruments will act as modifiers of the percentage impairment they are awarded, but the awards will, in general, primarily reflect objective factors. This is in keeping with the general strat-egy of the Guides to consider PRI but to limit the amount of impairment that is awarded for subjec-tive factors. In no circumstances should the PRIs developed using this chapter be considered as an add-on to impairment determinations based on the criteria listed in Chapters 4 to 17. In essence, the PRIs derived according to this chapter (see method-ology described in the next section) are determined in a stand-alone fashion.

3.3c Rating Impairment When Pain Is Not Accompanied by Objective Findings

In response to criticisms of the complexity of the PRI system developed for the previous edition of the Guides, the system to be used in the Guides’ Sixth Edition is simple. A patient is awarded a presumptive percentage WPI on the basis of his or her responses on the Pain Disability Questionnaire (PDQ; Appendixes 3-1 and 3-2 in Section 3.7).24 The PDQ was developed as a measure of func-tional status of patients with pain, such as those

with chronic disabling musculoskeletal disorders. The psychometric properties are excellent, demon-strating strong reliability, validity, and responsive-ness, relative to many other existing measures of functional status. The focus of the PDQ, much like other health inventories, is primarily on how pain affects disabilities and ADLs. Moreover, it is based on the earlier reviewed biopsychosocial approach to pain. Therefore, an important core of the PDQ will include psychosocial variables (which empirical research has consistently shown to play an integral role in the development and maintenance of chronic pain and disability.)6

The PDQ consists of 15 items that are scored on a 10-point scale, for a maximum total score of 150. In a subsequent study by Gatchel and colleagues,25 total PDQ score was broken down into 4 categories based on the maximum score (high pain and disabil-ity) of 150 and a minimum score of 0: mild (0–70); moderate (71–100); severe (101–130); and extreme (131–150). Results of this categorization showed a linear trend for decreasing positive outcomes (eg, return-to-work and work retention) as the PDQ score categories increased.

Using the PDQ scoring method, the examiner can then modify this presumptive award on the basis of his or her clinical assessment of the reliability of the patient’s self-reports and assigns a final PRI award. A cap of 3% WPI is used for conditions that are rated with the PRI system.

3.3d Steps of Assessment

1. Determine that the patient meets the general criteria for performing an impairment rating, as described in Chapter 2. In particular, determine that the patient is medically stable (ie, has reached Maximum Medical Improvement, or MMI).

2. Determine that the patient meets eligibility crite-ria for rating PRI. They are:

a. Pain has been determined to have a reasonable

3.4 Future Directions—Need for Research and Dialogue to Establish the Validity of Rating Pain-Related Impairment

Based on responses to Chapter 18 of the Guides’ Fifth Edition, we anticipate that responses to the PRI system outlined here will fall into familiar patterns. Skeptics of any system for rating PRI will attack the system for being unscientific and for violat-ing the principle that impairment ratings should be based on objective indexes of organ dysfunction. Proponents of PRI will attack the system for capping the size of PRI awards. In order to move past this fruitless dichotomy of opinion, we believe that it is crucially important to consider the issues underly-ing the dichotomy in a systematic way before the

Seventh Edition of the AMA Guides is developed. Specifically, we recommend the following:

1. Empirical research could be performed to deter-mine the strength of the independent contribution that pain makes to the burden of illness borne by individuals with various medical conditions and the ability of examiners to assess PRI reli-ably and validly. Considerable research has been done on the first issue, at least for some common painful conditions such as disorders of the lumbar spine.26 In contrast, we are not aware of system-atic research on the reliability of the PRI system developed for the Fifth Edition of the Guides, or of any other system for evaluating PRI. This issue should be explored empirically before another edition of the Guides is published.

2. As noted above, a striking feature of the “debate” over the appropriate role of PRI in the AMA Guides system is that, to date, there has been no real debate. We are not aware of any published article or symposium in which enthusiasts and skeptics have debated the appropriateness of PRI. It is time for such a debate to occur, so that the issues separating proponents and opponents can be articulated and methods of assessing the valid-ity of the arguments can be developed.

3.5 Conclusion

The stakes in deciding how and whether to include PRI in the Guides’ system are high. Discussions about PRI need to be framed within the broader context of discussions about the appropriate role of subjective factors in the evaluation of impair-ment and disability. Although pain is a commonly reported cause of activity limitation among indi-viduals undergoing rating of impairment with the AMA Guides, various other subjective experiences (eg, fatigue or fear of reinjury) can also act as bar-riers to activity. If these subjective factors are to be considered in impairment ratings, examiners have no choice but to rely at least in part on com-munications by patients about their experiences. Moreover, the assessment of psychiatric impairment relies heavily on communications by patients. Taken together, the above groups represent an enormous number of individuals whose activity limitations are incomprehensible if an impairment system relies strictly on objective medical factors and excludes reports by patients about their subjective experiences.

Everything about rating impairment in those with chronic pain engenders controversy except that the suffering of these individuals is real. Our view is that an enormous number of people are limited by “unbearable sensations” as they attempt to engage in activities27 and that these subjective factors cannot be fully assessed by any system that relies strictly on objective factors. The issue for the future will be to develop impairment rating systems that take into account both the importance of subjective fac-tors and the difficulties inherent in the evaluation of another person’s subjective experiences.

3.6 Examples

EXAMPLE 3-1 NON-SPECIFIC PAIN AFFECTING RIGHT LOWER EXTREMITY

A 43-year-old man reported ongoing burning pain in his right foot and ankle following an ankle sprain 3 years earlier. At the time of the initial injury, plain X rays of the ankle revealed no evidence of fracture. Subsequent plain X rays, a 3-phase bone scan, elec-tromyography (EMG) and nerve conduction velocity (NCV) testing, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the ankle are all without identifiable abnormalities. The man indicates that his symptoms become worse with weight-bearing activities and that he is significantly limited with respect to walking, climbing stairs, and prolonged standing. He reports ongoing, intermittent swelling associated with color and temperature asymmetries between the left and right ankles. He has no other pain complaints and no general medical problems. His physical examination is normal; there are no identifiable sensory abnor-malities, swelling, or color or temperature asym-metries when the affected and unaffected ankles are compared. The examiner judges him to be credible with respect to his pain complaints. His score on the Pain Disability Questionnaire is 72. The examiner concludes that the patient has moderate PRI and awards 1% WPI.

Comment: The pathophysiologic basis of this man’s pain is unknown; however, he reports a constellation of symptoms that are suggestive of complex regional pain syndrome, type 1. He does not, however, meet the diagnostic criteria for this as specified elsewhere in the Extremity Chapters. On physical examination and in all laboratory testing and imaging studies, there are no identifiable abnormalities. The exam-iner judges him to be credible, but there are no identifiable objective findings of organ or body part derangement. Thus, if he is to receive any

impairment rating, it is via the PRI system described in this chapter.

EXAMPLE 3-2 POST-CONCUSSIVE HEADACHE

A 34-year-old woman was involved in a motor vehicle accident 2 years ago. She struck her head against the windshield and reports that she awoke a “few seconds” later and felt “dazed.” She was taken by ambulance to an emergency room and was diagnosed with a “mild concussion.” Review of the emergency department records reveals a normal neurological assessment, including normal mental status. With the extent of the trauma and her reported loss of consciousness a head CT was performed which showed no evidence of fracture or intracranial pathology. Conservative management was recommended. Within the week following the accident she experienced difficulties with head-aches, felt “dizzy” at times, was irritable, felt her memory was not as sharp, and had difficulties with sleep. She returned to the emergency room 2 weeks post accident, had a normal examination and a repeat CT was normal. Her symptoms continued and she was referred to a neurologist six months post injury. The neurological assessment was normal. An MRI, cervical spine imaging, and neuropsychologi-cal evaluation were ordered; these studies were nor-mal. Over time her symptoms have improved, with the exception of her headaches. She reports having problems with headaches two to three times a week,

lasting a couple of hours at a time, and described as squeezing. Her primary treating physician has diag-nosed post-concussive headaches. She denies any history of prior headache and review of the medical records reveals no documentation of headaches prior to the accident. At the evaluation she reports that the headaches are very disabling when they occur and do appear to be stable in frequency and duration.

Her physical examination is normal; there are no neurological deficits and mental status is normal. She was felt to be very credible. The score on the Pain Disability Questionnaire is 120. The examiner concludes that the patient has severe PRI and awards 2% WPI.

Comment: Post-concussive headaches can be of mul-tifactorial origin and may take many forms. In addition to post-traumatic muscle tension-type headaches, they may mimic migraine. Post-traumatic migraine is not uncommon. This is thought to be due to injury to the vasonervorum and autonomic vascular instability.

Mixed tension and migraine is also commonly seen in patients with post-traumatic headache.

Other proposed causes have included direct or indi-rect traction injury to nerves, such as the occipital nerves. This may result in a more classically neuritic pain quality. She had no documented intracranial pathology and there have been no documented neu-rological deficits. There are no factors that would result in ratable impairment other than for pain.

Appendix 3-2 Pain Disability Questionnaire (PDQ)

Administering the Pain Disability Questionnaire

Follow these instructions for administering and scoring the PDQ:

1. Reproduce the PDQ (Appendix 3-1) and ask the patient to complete all items on the questionnaire.

2. If necessary, the patient may complete the form with the assistance of a translator or reader. Be certain all 15 questions are answered. If the patient is unable to complete the PDQ, no functional assessment score will be given.

3. The evaluating doctor will score the PDQ by adding together the marked integer in each question.

4. If the patient fails to mark a question, the default score for that question is 0.

5. Apply the final score to Table 3-1 and consider this in the Steps of Assessment as described in Section 3.3d.

The PDQ scores can be divided into 5 distinct categories: no disability (score of 0); mild (scores of 1 to 70); moderate (scores of 71 to 100); severe (scores of 101 to 130); and extreme (scores of 131 to 150).

Appendix 3-3 Additional Pain Considerations

The American Medical Association’s Guides to the Evaluation of Permanent Impairment, Sixth Edition is intended to provide a valid and clinically relevant source for assessing and rating an individual’s permanent impairment. With each edition, a group of clinical experts, representing various medical organizations, mounts a collective effort to update the Guides and refine its validity and practical clinical application. This effort is applied to each chapter to enhance the rel-evancy of impairment ratings, improve internal consistency, promote greater precision and simplify the rating process. However, in some situations marked by a lack of scientific evidence on which to base recommendations, Guides’ contribu-tors rely on clinical expertise. At times, clinical opinions differ, creating a situation where consensus is lacking.

The assessment of impairment associated with chronic pain is a clear example of the difficulties that arise when such differences in clinical opinion exist. Experts have disagreed about the usefulness and questioned the validity of the rating systems for pain-related impairment (PRI) described in previous editions of the Guides, and these difficulties have contin-ued throughout the development of the current chapter.

Here, the pain chapter authors provide a snapshot of the existing differences between proponents and opponents of developing a pain-related impairment (PRI) rating system and call for a comprehensive approach to address future devel-opment of a reliable Guides’ pain rating system.

Criticism of Earlier Editions of the Guides

Arguments in Favor of Including PRI

Pain specialists have advanced several reasons for including PRI in the Guides system, and for permitting high impairment percentages to be awarded on the basis of chronic pain:

• Pain affects a person’s ability to perform Activities of Daily Living (ADLs). This effect is to some extent independent of objective factors. Thus, even when a person has a condition associated with objective factors, statistical theory dictates that predictions regarding his/her ability to perform ADLs, based on an evaluation of both objective factors and pain, will be more accurate than predictions based on objective factors alone.

• Although chronic pain can sometimes be conceptualized as a “component” of a disorder with objective factors, it can also reflect a neurobiologic disease that is independent of a measurable organ/body part dysfunction. In sup-port of this conceptual model, proponents of PRI note that recent research on the pathophysiology of pain has cast doubt on the hypothesis that chronic pain is usually closely associated with tissue damage of dysfunction of organs/body parts. In particular, they cite research demonstrating nervous system sensitization, and note that clini-cal phenomena that are often dismissed as “not real” can be explained in terms of altered functioning at the level of the dorsal horn, thalamus, and sensory cortex. Congruent with this theoretical model, experience demonstrates that there are medical conditions with no associated objective factors in which pain influences a person’s ability to perform ADLs. Thus, it is appropriate to assess pain and its effects, even in individuals with no objective factors.

• The independent contribution of pain to ADL deficits can be substantial. Thus, the Guides should not only include a system for assessing PRI, but the system should permit examiners to award high whole person impairment percent-ages to patients on the basis of their pain.

Arguments Against the Inclusion of PRI in the Guides

We are not aware of any published manuscripts in which arguments against the inclusion of PRI have been articulated. Thus, we must construct these arguments on the basis of informal discussions with critics of PRI.

• The purpose of the Guides is to evaluate impairment on the basis of objective factors. Pain is a subjective factor, and is not a kind of impairment. Therefore, PRI should not be included in the Guides.

• There is no empirical evidence that demonstrates the reliability and validity of any system to rate PRI.

• It is redundant to develop a system for assessing pain, because pain has already been factored into the ratings that are described throughout the Guides.

• The PRI system described in Chapter 18 of the Guides, fifth edition was excessively complex and difficult to use.

• Assessing PRI is difficult; therefore, the inter-examiner reliability and validity of such assessments are likely to be low. The assessment of pain insinuates unscientific, subjective methods of impairment assessment into a system that is otherwise objective.

In light of the current controversy related to pain-related impairment, the Guides, 6th edition Editorial Panel determined that a 3% whole person impairment will be used for conditions that are rated with the PRI system. This decision was based on the tenet that in the absence of objective data, recommendations will be based on precedent. In this case, the 3% WPI is based on that used in the fifth edition of the Guides.

The authors of the Pain chapter have made various recommendations for research and collaboration between opponents and proponents of PRI, in order to build a foundation for the pain chapter in the Guides seventh edition. We hope that these recommendations are implemented to form a common ground based on objective evidence.

In light of the current controversy related to pain-related impairment, the Guides, 6th edition Editorial Panel determined that a 3% whole person impairment will be used for conditions that are rated with the PRI system. This decision was based on the tenet that in the absence of objective data, recommendations will be based on precedent. In this case, the 3% WPI is based on that used in the fifth edition of the Guides.

The authors of the Pain chapter have made various recommendations for research and collaboration between opponents and proponents of PRI, in order to build a foundation for the pain chapter in the Guides seventh edition. We hope that these recommendations are implemented to form a common ground based on objective evidence.
